Nous sommes des étudiants de EPITA de la majeure SCIA. 

Nous ne brassons pas d'Euler.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a web app that turns twenty years of NASA microgravity combustion experiments into answers about fire safety in space.

  • Data pipeline. A Python pipeline reads all 19 combustion experiments of NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database through its public API. It merges their 21 test tables into one harmonised table of about 3,400 tests, with the same columns everywhere: oxygen %, pressure in psi, airflow, material, outcome and burn time.
  • Filling the gaps. Missing values come from PSI documents, extracted with OCR, and from raw telemetry: FLEX-2 chamber readings and ACME chamber pressure files. Every value records where it came from: measured, document or team assumption. Nothing is invented.
  • Explore. An interactive map plots every test by oxygen and pressure, with the zone of each habitat drawn on it.
  • Data. Experiments are ranked for four habitats (ISS, lunar base, NASA exploration atmosphere, spacesuit). The rank counts the measured tests that ran in air at least as favourable to fire as the habitat’s. It uses NASA’s pressure-equivalence relation (Hirsch et al.), with no arbitrary weights.
  • Compare. Up to four experiments side by side.
  • Simulator. An animated cabin where you set oxygen, pressure, gravity, fuel and airflow. The flame’s behaviour (holds, goes out, smokes) comes only from the closest real NASA tests, which are cited below it. Where no test exists, it shows a question mark instead of a guess.
  • Cosmo. A mascot assistant powered by Claude. It answers questions from PSI records, 264 publications (OpenAlex) and 40 NASA NTRS reports, cites its sources and can drive the interface.

Benefits and intended impact

The app shows quickly what has and has not been tested. Its key finding: future lunar habitats will breathe 30–34% oxygen, yet no real solid material has been tested in microgravity above 22.7%, and PSI holds no partial-gravity test at all.

Mission planners, researchers and students get a clear map of these gaps, the experiments to read first for each habitat, and a list of what to test next. Harmonised data can be downloaded as CSV for predictive modelling.

Tools and technologies

  • Back end: Python with uv, pandas, NumPy, FastAPI and Pydantic. Tests run with pytest and code style is checked with ruff.
  • Front end: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript modules, with hand-built SVG charts and animations, and French/English text.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) for the Cosmo assistant and as a coding assistant.
  • Data sources: NASA PSI API, NASA NTRS API, OpenAlex API, plus OCR on PSI documents.
  • Collaboration: GitHub, with pull requests and code review.
  • Hardware: standard laptops only.

Creativity

  • A simulator grounded in evidence. It is not a physics engine, but it is honest: every animation comes from cited tests.
  • A ranking that explains itself. Each rank comes with a sentence giving the fact behind it.
  • A mascot that sees your page. Cosmo can show you the answer in the interface.
  • Unpublished data recovered. Raw telemetry files nobody had linked to the test tables supply real pressures and outcomes.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: we trace the origin of every value and never fill a gap silently.
    • inverse flames are excluded from habitat comparisons, because their oxygen value is the burner stream;
    • smoke and dust experiments (SAME, SAME-R, DAFT) are separated from fires;
    • duplicate records are removed.
  • Known limits: the pressure-equivalence relation comes from solid materials tested in Earth gravity, so applying it to gases, droplets and microgravity is an extrapolation, stated on the Method page.
  • Accessibility: keyboard navigation, screen-reader text and reduced-motion support.
  • Reach: the app is bilingual, French and English.
